output.title: Design for vendor price changes before they bite
output.body:
If you run a small business, vendor pricing changes are not really a finance story. They are a workflow control story.

The practical question is simple: which recurring process depends on a tool you do not control? Invoicing, customer reply triage, and data entry are the usual places to look, because a price change there can quietly turn a workable setup into a weak one. Don’t start with a grand strategy memo. Start with one workflow and one vendor.

Write down three things: the current rate, what triggers a review, and whether that step could be swapped out or rebuilt later. That gives you a clear view of where a price rise is merely annoying and where it would force a real change in process. The goal is not to predict every future increase; the goal is to know which increase would matter.

If you want a bounded decision, use this rule: keep the vendor when the change is absorbable, and treat it as a replacement candidate when the cost sits inside a repeatable workflow you rely on every week. If automation is ever chosen, keep money movement and other high-risk decisions under human approval. That part should stay boring. Boring is useful.

For a one-person audit, a quarterly check of rate changes and swap thresholds is enough to keep the decision in your hands.
